key_insight: Visual similarity is not one-size-fits-all: people judge images differently depending on the aspect they care about, such as shape, color, or texture. This paper shows that perceptual metrics should be conditioned on the requested sense of similarity instead of collapsing everything into a single score.
problem_solved: Existing image similarity metrics produce a single scalar value, which cannot capture context-dependent human judgments. The paper addresses the lack of benchmark data and models that can evaluate similarity across multiple semantic aspects in a flexible, text-guided way.
method: Build a large-scale dataset of human annotations on image triplets, where each triplet is labeled across multiple free-form similarity aspects.
Introduce a text-prompted perceptual metric that takes a natural-language description of the desired similarity aspect as input.
Benchmark the approach against existing perceptual similarity methods to evaluate how well they match human judgments under different similarity criteria.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this enables more human-aligned evaluation of generated or edited images when the relevant notion of similarity depends on the task. It is especially useful for image generation, editing, retrieval, and evaluation workflows where shape, color, style, or other factors may matter differently.

paper_title: The Many Senses of Visual Similarity: A Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Metric
paper_authors: Sheng-Yu Wang, Yotam Nitzan, Aaron Hertzmann, Jun-Yan Zhu, Eli Shechtman
